A similar safeguard of the interests of the people is involved in the question we are now discussing. The procedure as outlined in the Civil Service Act requires that there shall be first a report of the deputy head in writing, setting out the reasons why the additional clerkship is required. That safeguard is required because of the political influences that are apt to surround the head of the department. It is no secret in public life that ministers of the Crown are besieged by office-seekers, and it was thought wise that some one, removed from the political arena, and who has immediate supervision and control of the department, should be the one to recommend that an additional clerkship is required. Then, after the head of the department has passed upon the report and submitted it to council, and the council has approved of it, the final determination is left with parliament, the people's representatives in the House of Commons. It is said that the reason for the additional clerkship will be given after the vote is taken. But what possible benefit could there be in stating the reasons then. The deputy head would simply say that the money having been voted by parliament, all he had to do was to recommend the additional new clerk. The abuses that could creep in if such a course were followed are innumerable. I need only mention one. A minister of the Crown may have relatives,-which is something not unknown to the present administration,-he may have nephews, sons and others who would he of inestimable value to the public service in his estimation, but who would hamper and impede the administration of the department in the opinion of the deputy head, and they may be the last persons
